<noinclude><pagequality level="2" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader||STRENGTH OF MATERIALS|1013}}</noinclude> as wrought iron the elastic extension is only about <math>\tfrac{1}{12000}</math> of the length for each ton per square inch of load, and the whole amount up to the elastic limit is perhaps <math>\tfrac{1}{1000}</math> of the length; with a length of 8 in., which is usual in tensile tests, it is desirable to read the extension to, say, <math>\tfrac{1}{50000}</math> in. if the modulus of elasticity is to be found with fair accuracy, or if the limits of proportionality between strain to stress are under examination. Measurements taken between marks on one side of the bar only are liable to be affected by bending of the piece, and it is essential either to make independent measurements on both sides or to measure the displacement between two pieces which are attached to the bar in such a manner as to share equally the strain on both sides.

[[File:eb1911 v25 p1039 c1f1.png|center|266px]]

{{smaller block|In experiments carried out by Bauschinger, independent measurements of the strains on both sides of the bar were made by using mirror micrometers of the type illustrated diagrammatically in fig. 15. Two clips <math>a</math> and <math>b</math> clasp the test-piece at the place between which the extension is to be measured.}}

[[File:eb1911 v25 p1039 c2f1.png|center|350px]]
{{c|{{sc|Fig.}} 15.}}

{{smaller block|The clip <math>b</math> carries two small rollers <math>d_1</math> <math>d_2</math> which are free to rotate on centres fixed in the clip. These rollers press on two plane strips <math>c_1</math> <math>c_2</math> attached to the other clip. When the specimen is stretched the rollers consequently turn through angles proportional to the strain, and the amount of turning is read by means of small mirrors <math>g_1</math> and <math>g_2</math>, fixed to the rollers, which reflect the divisions of a fixed scale <math>f</math> into the reading telescopes <math>e_1</math> <math>e_2</math>. In Martens's extensometer each of the rollers is replaced by a rhombic piece of steel with sharp edges, one of which bears against the test-piece, while the other rests in a groove formed in the spring projecting parallel to the test-piece from the distant clip. Much excellent work has been done by extensometers of this class, but in point of convenience of manipulation it is of great advantage to have the apparatus self-contained.}}

[[File:eb1911 v25 p1039 c2f2.png|center|201px]]
{{c|{{sc|Fig.}} 16.}}

{{smaller block|J. A. Ewing has introduced a microscope extensometer of the self-contained type which is shown in fig. 16; its action will be seen by reference to the diagram fig. 17.}}

[[File:eb1911 v25 p1039 c2f3.png|center|166px]]
{{c|{{sc|Fig.}} 17.}}

{{smaller block|Two clips <math>\text{B}</math> and <math>\text{C}</math> are secured on the bar, each by means of a pair of opposed set-screws. Between the two is a rod <math>\text{B}'</math> which is hinged to <math>\text{B}</math> and has a blunt pointed upper end which makes a ball-and-socket joint with <math>\text{C}</math> at <math>\text{P}</math>. Another bar <math>\text{R}</math> hangs from <math>\text{C}</math>, and carries a mark which is read by a microscope attached to <math>\text{B}</math>. Hence, when the specimen stretches, the length of <math>\text{B}'</math> being fixed, the bar <math>\text{R}</math> is pulled up relatively to the microscope, and the amount of the movement is measured by a micrometer scale in the eyepiece.
